podcast.body: An original copy of "The White Album" from 1968, distinguished by its unique sequential serial number embossed on the front. EMI's numbering system meant the very first copy, 0000001, was owned by Ringo Starr. In 2015, Starr sold his perfect-condition copy at auction, with the proceeds benefiting his charity, The Lotus Foundation. It fetched $790,000 US dollars, setting an all-time record for an album at that time. "His serial number on his white album was 000000000001."

podcast.body: On this album, John Lennon included the song "Sexy Sadie," which was a disguised diss track. Lennon initially wanted to title the song "Maharishi" as a direct kiss-off to the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, whom the group had recently distanced themselves from due to a sexual transgression. George Harrison, however, convinced Lennon to change the title to "Sexy Sadie" because it had the same number of syllables. "On the white album in 1968, for example, Sexy Sadie was a kiss off to the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi."

podcast.body: The Beatles' self-titled "White Album" was released coincidentally around the same time as The Rolling Stones' *Beggar's Banquet*. This synchronicity was notable because both albums featured minimalist white covers, though The Rolling Stones' white cover was a result of censorship. "coincidía con el lanzamiento del guay de Albueno de los Beatles."

The retail version of _The White Album_ is highly collectible because each record has a unique serial number. The first four records (numbers 0000001 through 0000004) were given to the individual Beatles members. Ringo Starr's copy, number 0000001, was sold for charity in 2015 for $790,000. "Every single one of those records has a serial number with the first four records going to each of the Beatles."

podcast.body: This album contains the song "Helter Skelter," which Charles Manson interpreted as a secret message from The Beatles. Manson believed the band was encouraging him to initiate a race war, a belief that ultimately culminated in the Tate-LaBianca murders in 1969. "Charles Manson believed that the Beatles were speaking to him through the song Helter Skelter from the White Album."

podcast.body: This album marks the point up to which The Beatles recorded their music primarily in mono. Despite recording in mono, these masters were often re-channeled into "fake stereo" for stereo record releases, as stereo records were perceived as superior. "The Beatles, for example, recorded in mono all the way through to the white album."
